options.a: A reasonable suspicion that a crime may have occurred
options.b: A crime committed in your presence or the state's exact rule
options.c: A supervisor's verbal approval before making the arrest
options.d: A written complaint signed by the property owner

distractorExplanations.a: Reasonable suspicion is the lower police stop standard; a citizen's arrest needs an offense seen or the state's specific rule.
distractorExplanations.c: A supervisor cannot authorize an arrest the law does not allow; the legal basis comes from state statute.
distractorExplanations.d: A signed owner complaint starts a police case; it does not by itself give a guard arrest authority.

options.a: Grounds to detain them until they sign a statement
options.b: A civil matter that police will not respond to
options.c: A reason to call police if they will not leave
options.d: Only a violation if a sign is posted at the entry

distractorExplanations.a: Trespass lets you ask them to leave and call police; holding someone for a signed statement risks false imprisonment.
distractorExplanations.b: Refusing to leave after consent is withdrawn is criminal trespass in most states, and police do respond.
distractorExplanations.d: A clear verbal withdrawal of consent is notice in itself; posted signage is a separate way to give notice.

options.a: The manager's instruction and a reasonable hunch
options.b: Police-style questioning until a confession
options.c: A set one-hour hold before anyone calls police
options.d: Post orders and probable-cause standards

distractorExplanations.a: A hunch plus a manager's say-so is not probable cause; shopkeeper detention needs observed facts.
distractorExplanations.b: Guards detain briefly and hand off to police; extracting a confession by interrogation exceeds the role.
distractorExplanations.c: Merchant detention must be reasonable in time; police are called promptly, not after a fixed hold.

options.a: A police interrogation issue
options.b: Required before any guard detention
options.c: Read by guards before asking questions
options.d: A guard's duty at any stop

distractorExplanations.b: Miranda applies to custodial interrogation by government agents; private guards do not issue it at detention.
distractorExplanations.c: Private security officers are generally not state actors, so they do not read Miranda before questions.
distractorExplanations.d: Miranda is triggered by police custodial interrogation, not by a private guard's stop or contact.

options.a: Carrying a radio and a flashlight
options.b: Carrying a firearm or acting as armed
options.c: Controlling access at entry points
options.d: Writing incident and patrol reports

distractorExplanations.a: Radios and flashlights are standard unarmed-post equipment; only weapons need an armed license.
distractorExplanations.c: Access control is a core unarmed guard duty; it does not require an armed guard card.
distractorExplanations.d: Incident and patrol reports are part of every unarmed post; reporting is the unarmed officer's main tool.

options.a: The subject later files a formal complaint
options.b: You call police to take the report
options.c: You put hands on someone or they are injured
options.d: Your supervisor asks you for a written account

distractorExplanations.a: The report is triggered by the force or injury itself, not by whether the subject later complains.
distractorExplanations.b: Calling police does not replace your own use-of-force report; you document any contact you made.
distractorExplanations.d: Use-of-force reports are mandatory after physical contact or injury, not only when a supervisor asks.

options.a: Leave your post and something foreseeable happens
options.b: Call 911 before you notify your supervisor
options.c: Write a report that is later used in court
options.d: Refuse a client request that breaks post orders

distractorExplanations.b: Calling 911 first in an emergency is reasonable care; it reduces rather than raises your liability.
distractorExplanations.c: An accurate report used in court protects you; liability comes from negligence, not documentation.
distractorExplanations.d: Declining a request that violates post orders is following your duty; abandoning the post is the risk.

unarmed-security-officer-readiness-check.explanation: Foreseeability. This item asks: “Liability is highest when you:”. The matching answer is: Leave your post and something foreseeable happens, or you use illegal force. Independent UniPrep diagnostic — not an official unarmed guard paper. Using illegal force also creates high personal and employer liability.

options.a: Your call to confiscate their ID and keep it
options.b: A document-and-manager/police issue
options.c: A server's issue that security stays out of
options.d: Handled by a warning if they finish quickly

distractorExplanations.a: Guards may refuse entry or service, but keeping someone's ID is not authorized; document and escalate.
distractorExplanations.c: Security on licensed premises shares responsibility for underage drinking; it must report and document.
distractorExplanations.d: Letting a minor finish the drink keeps the violation going; stop service, document, notify a manager.

options.a: Fine to share once you leave the job
options.b: Shareable if you leave out names
options.c: Not for social media or friends
options.d: Public after your shift ends

distractorExplanations.a: Confidentiality obligations usually survive employment; leaving the job does not release client secrets.
distractorExplanations.b: Removing names does not make client information safe; details alone can identify the site and risk.
distractorExplanations.d: Information stays confidential off duty; the end of a shift does not make it public.

options.a: Block an exit with no legal basis
options.b: Ask someone to wait for police on a good detention
options.c: Ask a trespasser to leave the property
options.d: Follow a suspect at a distance outside

distractorExplanations.c: Asking a trespasser to leave restricts no one's movement; false imprisonment requires confinement.
distractorExplanations.d: Observing a suspect from a distance does not confine them, so it is not false imprisonment.
distractorExplanations.b: “Ask someone to wait for police on a good detention” does not answer “False imprisonment risk appears when you:”. The matching answer is: Block an exit with no legal basis.

options.a: Allowed under your guard card
options.b: Not your unarmed guard job
options.c: Part of mobile patrol duties
options.d: Covered by post orders

distractorExplanations.a: A guard card does not license process serving or bail recovery; those need separate licenses.
distractorExplanations.c: Mobile patrol checks client properties; serving papers or recovering fugitives is a different job.
distractorExplanations.d: Post orders cannot grant authority the license lacks; process serving needs its own credential.

options.a: The official state guard card licensing exam
options.b: An approved state pre-licensing training course
options.c: Independent practice — not a state guard card exam
options.d: A firearms qualification for an armed guard card

distractorExplanations.a: This is an independent UniPrep practice mock; official guard card exams are run by the state agency.
distractorExplanations.b: Pre-licensing training must be completed with a state-approved school; this mock is self-study practice.
distractorExplanations.d: This mock covers unarmed duties only; firearms qualification is a separate armed-license course.

options.a: The same fixed route at set times for consistency
options.b: Fast enough to hit every checkpoint in record time
options.c: Focused on the lobby camera monitor, not walking
options.d: Irregular enough to be unpredictable, with eyes up

distractorExplanations.a: A fixed route at set times lets offenders time your rounds; patrols should vary in timing and path.
distractorExplanations.b: Racing checkpoints means you scan tags without observing; patrol quality comes from looking, not speed.
distractorExplanations.c: Camera watching does not replace foot patrol; you need to see, smell and hear conditions in person.

options.a: Lighting and a radio check
options.b: Going in dark to surprise anyone
options.c: A solo sweep before calling in
options.d: Propping the door for later

distractorExplanations.b: Entering without light raises trip and ambush risk; light the space and tell dispatch first.
distractorExplanations.c: Searching alone before calling in leaves no one aware of your location; radio first, per policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Propping a stairwell door defeats fire separation and access control; it is not a safety step.

options.a: Waving in faces you know
options.b: Badges and tailgating
options.c: Logging only VIP visitors
options.d: Patrolling the perimeter

distractorExplanations.a: Waving in familiar faces bypasses badge checks; policy requires each person to badge in.
distractorExplanations.c: Access control logs every visitor, not just VIPs; partial logs leave gaps in who is on site.
distractorExplanations.d: Perimeter patrol is a separate duty; access control is checking credentials at entry points.

options.a: Left open and noted at the end of shift
options.b: Locked quietly with no report needed
options.c: Secured if safe, documented, and reported
options.d: Reported to the client by email next week

distractorExplanations.a: An unsecured door is a live risk; secure it now if safe, rather than noting it hours later.
distractorExplanations.b: Locking without reporting hides a possible breach or broken hardware; every finding is documented.
distractorExplanations.d: A week's delay leaves the client unaware of a breach; report it during the shift it was found.

options.a: Replacing foot patrols
options.b: Fire and smoke detection
options.c: Tracking guard breaks
options.d: Review and deterrence

distractorExplanations.a: CCTV supplements patrols; cameras miss smells, sounds and blind spots that foot patrol catches.
distractorExplanations.b: Fire and smoke detection is the job of the fire alarm system, not security cameras.
distractorExplanations.c: CCTV exists to protect the site through review and deterrence, not mainly to time guard breaks.

options.a: Approached with caution and backup as orders say
options.b: Entered alone at once to catch any intruder
options.c: Logged as a likely false alarm for day shift
options.d: Reset at the panel before anyone checks it

distractorExplanations.b: Rushing in alone ignores backup procedures; approach with caution and notify per post orders.
distractorExplanations.c: Treat each alarm as real until checked; deferring it to day shift leaves a possible intrusion open.
distractorExplanations.d: Resetting before checking erases the alarm cause; respond to the location first, then reset per SOP.

options.a: A reason to shelter in the car all shift
options.b: More slips and more HVAC/roof issues
options.c: Fewer patrols since crime drops in rain
options.d: Radio silence to save batteries

distractorExplanations.a: Bad weather adjusts how you patrol, not whether you patrol; you still cover the post.
distractorExplanations.c: Weather raises hazards like leaks and slips that patrols must catch; it is not a reason to cut rounds.
distractorExplanations.d: Weather increases risk, so radio contact matters more; carry spare batteries instead of going silent.

options.a: Opened carefully to check the contents
options.b: Moved outside to a safer spot
options.c: A bomb-procedure / do-not-touch issue
options.d: Left alone with no report needed

distractorExplanations.a: Suspicious packages are not opened by guards; follow do-not-touch and evacuation procedures.
distractorExplanations.b: Moving a suspicious item can trigger it; isolate the area and leave the package in place.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaving it unreported ignores the threat; clear the area and notify supervisor and police.

options.a: On a labeled hook at the desk
options.b: Left in the door for next shift
options.c: Under the desk mat
options.d: On your person or in the box

distractorExplanations.a: A labeled hook at an open desk breaks key control; signed-out keys stay on you or in the lockbox.
distractorExplanations.b: Keys left in a door give anyone access; hand-offs go through the key log or lockbox.
distractorExplanations.c: Hiding keys under a mat is a known spot thieves check; key control means on you or in the box.

options.a: Closed and reported
options.b: Left open for airflow
options.c: Tied open more firmly
options.d: Noted for next week

distractorExplanations.b: Fire doors must stay closed to stop smoke spread; airflow is never a valid reason to wedge one.
distractorExplanations.c: Fastening a fire door open defeats the fire separation; it must be released and closed.
distractorExplanations.d: A wedged fire door is an immediate life-safety hazard; close it now and report it this shift.

options.a: Fine until the next audit
options.b: A work order and extra patrol
options.c: A reason to skip that lot
options.d: Only the landlord's concern

distractorExplanations.a: Dark lots invite crime now; lighting outages get a work order and extra patrol, not a wait.
distractorExplanations.c: Dark areas need more patrol presence, not less, until the lighting is repaired.
distractorExplanations.d: Guards report lighting failures as security risks; it is not left solely to the landlord to notice.

options.a: Opinions on who is guilty
options.b: Site alarm codes and passwords
options.c: Times, names, and facts
options.d: Summaries written next day

distractorExplanations.a: Notes record observed facts; guesses about guilt undermine your credibility in court.
distractorExplanations.b: Writing alarm codes in a notebook that can be lost or subpoenaed is a security breach.
distractorExplanations.d: Notes are written as events happen; next-day summaries lose accurate times and details.

options.a: Let in if carrying tools
options.b: Detained until police arrive
options.c: Given a master key
options.d: Stopped and verified

distractorExplanations.a: Tools and uniforms are easy props for intruders; verify identity and authorization before entry.
distractorExplanations.b: No badge is not a crime; challenge and verify the visitor rather than detaining them.
distractorExplanations.c: Issuing master keys to an unverified person breaks key control and creates major liability.

options.a: Shorter steps and reporting the ice
options.b: Long strides to cross the ice fast
options.c: Hands in pockets to stay warm
options.d: Skipping the patrol without reporting it

distractorExplanations.b: Long fast strides raise slip risk on ice; short flat-footed steps keep your balance.
distractorExplanations.c: Hands in pockets stop you from breaking a fall; keep hands free and use gloves instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Skipping rounds silently leaves the post uncovered; report the hazard and adjust the route.

options.a: Physically stopping the suspect yourself
options.b: Calling police when there is a crime in progress
options.c: Finishing your patrol loop before calling
options.d: Filming the crime instead of calling for help

distractorExplanations.a: Observe-and-report posts call police; physical intervention exceeds most unarmed post orders.
distractorExplanations.c: A crime in progress takes priority over the patrol route; call police immediately.
distractorExplanations.d: Video can help, but the duty is to call police first; filming does not replace reporting.

options.a: Silence the panel, then investigate the source alone
options.b: Use the elevators to move people out of the building faster
options.c: Evacuate per plan, close doors if safe, meet the fire dept
options.d: Wait for a second alarm or call to confirm there is a fire

distractorExplanations.a: Silencing the panel with smoke showing delays evacuation; guards follow the evacuation plan first.
distractorExplanations.b: Elevators can stop or open onto fire floors; evacuation uses the stairs unless fire service directs.
distractorExplanations.d: Visible smoke already confirms the fire; waiting for another alarm wastes escape time.

options.a: Drive the person to the ER yourself
options.b: Wait to see if the chest pain passes
options.c: Move them before calling anyone
options.d: 911, AED if trained, crowd control

distractorExplanations.a: Driving a patient yourself delays EMS care and adds liability; call 911 and wait with them.
distractorExplanations.b: Chest pain may be a heart attack; delay worsens outcomes, so call 911 right away.
distractorExplanations.c: Moving a patient first can worsen injuries; call 911, then move only if the scene is unsafe.

options.a: Run/hide/help others as trained
options.b: Confront the attacker with your flashlight
options.c: Search rooms to locate the shooter
options.d: Gather everyone in the lobby

distractorExplanations.b: Unarmed officers avoid engaging; confronting is a last resort only when life is in immediate danger.
distractorExplanations.c: Searching for the attacker is a police task; unarmed guards evacuate, lock down and inform.
distractorExplanations.d: Massing people in one open area makes them a target; follow run/hide plans and lockdown rooms.

options.a: Ended quickly so the phone line stays free for police calls
options.b: Kept on the line if possible, notes taken, supervisor/police
options.c: Handled by pulling the fire alarm to empty the building now
options.d: Transferred to the client so management decides what to do

distractorExplanations.a: Keeping the caller talking gathers clues on location, timing and voice; hanging up loses them.
distractorExplanations.c: Pulling the fire alarm may route people past the device; evacuation is a supervisor/police decision.
distractorExplanations.d: The call taker fills out the threat checklist; transferring the caller risks losing them entirely.

options.a: Reset the fire pumps and alarm panel to restore power
options.b: Send everyone home and lock the building until power returns
options.c: Check emergency lighting, elevators, and the generator plan
options.d: Use the elevators to check each floor for problems

distractorExplanations.a: Fire pumps and panels are not power resets; tampering with them can disable life-safety systems.
distractorExplanations.b: Evacuation decisions follow the site plan; first check lighting, elevators and the generator.
distractorExplanations.d: Elevators may stall during a power failure; check for entrapments rather than riding them.

options.a: Find the source and wipe it up with a mop
options.b: Hose down the area before reading the SDS
options.c: Ventilate by propping doors and keep working
options.d: Isolate, evacuate as trained, call specialists

distractorExplanations.a: Unknown chemicals can be toxic or reactive; cleanup is for trained HAZMAT responders.
distractorExplanations.b: Water can react with some chemicals; the SDS and specialists decide the cleanup method.
distractorExplanations.c: Propping doors can spread fumes through the building; isolate the area and evacuate.

options.a: Widen, communicate, call for more staff
options.b: Close the gate to stop the crowd's push
options.c: Push back the front line to make space
options.d: Cut the lights to calm the crowd down

distractorExplanations.b: Closing the gate during a surge builds pressure and causes crush injuries; open and widen flow.
distractorExplanations.c: Pushing the front row compresses the crowd further; relieve pressure from behind instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Darkness causes panic and trips in a crowd; keep lighting on and give clear directions.

options.a: Wait 30 minutes before calling a code
options.b: Code/description, exits, cameras
options.c: A store-by-store search before any code
options.d: Page the child's name and wait at the desk

distractorExplanations.a: Missing-child codes are called immediately; minutes of delay let a child leave the building.
distractorExplanations.c: Searching store by store before a code leaves exits uncovered; call the code first.
distractorExplanations.d: Paging alone is passive; the code covers exits and cameras while staff search.

options.a: Move people to their cars to drive away
options.b: Move people outside to the open lot
options.c: Move people to the marked shelter area
options.d: Move people to the top floor for safety

distractorExplanations.a: Vehicles offer little protection in a tornado; shelter in the lowest interior marked area.
distractorExplanations.b: Open areas expose people to flying debris; shelter indoors in the lowest interior space.
distractorExplanations.d: Upper floors take the most wind damage; tornado shelter is the lowest interior level.

options.a: Pry the doors open to free them quickly
options.b: Climb in through the hatch to help them
options.c: Wait an hour before calling for help
options.d: Call the service/fire number, talk calmly

distractorExplanations.a: Prying elevator doors risks falls into the shaft; only elevator techs or firefighters free riders.
distractorExplanations.b: Entering through the hatch is dangerous and untrained; call the elevator service or fire department.
distractorExplanations.c: Entrapped riders may have medical needs; call the service or fire number right away.

options.a: PPE and the bloodborne kit
options.b: A dry mop and regular trash bags
options.c: Paper towels with bare hands
options.d: Leave it for the morning crew

distractorExplanations.b: Blood is regulated waste under OSHA's bloodborne pathogens rule; use the kit and biohazard bags.
distractorExplanations.c: Bare-hand contact risks bloodborne infection; gloves and other PPE are required.
distractorExplanations.d: A blood spill in a public lobby is an exposure risk; isolate it and clean it with the BBP kit now.

options.a: Stay put until radios work
options.b: Use the backup phone list
options.c: Leave post to find a supervisor
options.d: Use your personal social media

distractorExplanations.a: Waiting with no comms leaves you dark in an emergency; switch to the backup method at once.
distractorExplanations.c: Leaving the post abandons coverage; use backup phones to reach the supervisor instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Social media is not a secure or official channel; use the site's backup communication plan.

options.a: Go in alone to negotiate and calm everyone down
options.b: Pull the fire alarm so everyone leaves the building
options.c: Distance, call police, stop other traffic into the area
options.d: Wait to confirm the rumor before calling police

distractorExplanations.a: Negotiation is for trained police; entering alone can add another hostage.
distractorExplanations.b: A fire alarm sends people toward the danger and may provoke the subject; let police direct.
distractorExplanations.d: Police can verify the threat; delaying the call until you confirm it wastes critical time.

options.a: A text summary to coworkers
options.b: A report written at the end of the week
options.c: Deleting footage not tied to the event
options.d: A written timeline while it is fresh

distractorExplanations.a: Informal texts are not an official record; write a timed report while memory is fresh.
distractorExplanations.b: Waiting a week loses details and credibility; reports are written the same shift.
distractorExplanations.c: Footage after a major event may be evidence; preserve it and let investigators decide relevance.

options.a: Check it — stolen AEDs are a thing
options.b: Ignore it unless a patient is nearby
options.c: Silence it and log a false alarm
options.d: Reset it and walk away without looking

distractorExplanations.b: An AED cabinet alarm may mean the unit was taken; a missing AED matters before a patient appears.
distractorExplanations.c: Logging it as false without checking may leave the site without an AED; verify the unit is there.
distractorExplanations.d: Resetting without looking skips the check; confirm the AED is present and report if it is missing.

options.a: You write it before your shift ends
options.b: You wait until next week to write a use-of-force
options.c: You call your supervisor before you start writing it up
options.d: You attach the camera clip references

distractorExplanations.a: Writing before the shift ends is on time; use-of-force reports belong in the same shift.
distractorExplanations.c: Notifying a supervisor first is proper practice and does not make the report late.
distractorExplanations.d: Adding camera references strengthens a report; lateness is about waiting days to write it.

options.a: Fine if the post is quiet
options.b: Allowed if alarms are on
options.c: A firing and a liability
options.d: A minor write-up only

distractorExplanations.a: A quiet post still depends on your detection; sleeping leaves the site unprotected.
distractorExplanations.b: Alarms do not replace an awake officer; sleeping on post is a firing-level breach.
distractorExplanations.d: Sleeping on post is treated as serious misconduct and liability, not a minor write-up.

options.a: A tip if no one is hurt
options.b: Okay if you report it later
options.c: A minor policy issue
options.d: A crime and a fireable

distractorExplanations.a: Taking money to ignore a truck is bribery and theft facilitation, whether or not anyone is hurt.
distractorExplanations.b: Reporting afterward does not undo accepting a bribe; refuse it and report the offer at once.
distractorExplanations.c: Accepting a bribe to look away is a crime, not just a policy violation.

options.a: A security breach
options.b: Fine if faces are blurred
options.c: Good site marketing
options.d: A minor HR issue

distractorExplanations.b: Blurring faces does not protect badge equipment details; posting site systems is still a breach.
distractorExplanations.c: Posting badge equipment shows attackers how to clone access; it is a breach, not marketing.
distractorExplanations.d: Leaking access-control details is a security breach that can cost the contract, not a minor HR issue.

options.a: Legal if it is in post orders
options.b: Discrimination and a lawsuit
options.c: Good risk-based profiling
options.d: Fine if done politely

distractorExplanations.a: Post orders cannot authorize race-based stops; civil rights law overrides them.
distractorExplanations.c: Risk-based screening relies on behavior, not race; race-only stops are discrimination.
distractorExplanations.d: Politeness does not cure a discriminatory stop; selecting people by race is the violation.

options.a: No disclosure if off duty
options.b: Approval from the client
options.c: Keeping it secret at work
options.d: Disclosure per policy

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosure policies cover relationships between coworkers, even when dating happens off duty.
distractorExplanations.b: Relationship disclosure goes to your employer's HR or supervisor, not the client.
distractorExplanations.c: Secrecy is what policy prohibits; undisclosed pairs on one shift create fatigue and favoritism risk.

options.a: Outside the post and a safety crime waiting
options.b: Fine if you hold a forklift card
options.c: Allowed after hours when no one is around
options.d: A perk if the client does not find out

distractorExplanations.b: Holding a forklift card does not authorize using client equipment outside your post duties.
distractorExplanations.c: After-hours use with no one around raises the injury risk; equipment use is outside the post.
distractorExplanations.d: Using client property secretly is misconduct and possible theft of services, not a perk.

options.a: Reported at shift end
options.b: Reported immediately
options.c: Replaced with your phone
options.d: Noted in next week's log

distractorExplanations.a: A lost radio can be monitored by others; report it immediately, not at the end of the shift.
distractorExplanations.c: A phone does not replace secure site comms; the loss must still be reported immediately.
distractorExplanations.d: A week's delay lets an outsider listen to site traffic; lost radios are reported immediately.

options.a: Mention your employer's name to friends at a party
options.b: Apply for a job with a different guard company in town
options.c: Talk about the client's incoming shipment on a podcast
options.d: Post a photo of your own car on social media

distractorExplanations.a: Saying who you work for is normally fine; disclosing client operational details is the breach.
distractorExplanations.b: Job hunting is your right; the confidentiality duty covers client information, not your career.
distractorExplanations.d: Posting your own car is personal; the duty is not to share client security details.

options.a: You delete it as told
options.b: You keep a copy, then delete it
options.c: You blur it before saving
options.d: You refuse and escalate

distractorExplanations.a: Deleting footage of an incident is spoliation of evidence; a supervisor's order does not excuse it.
distractorExplanations.b: Keeping a private copy still destroys the official record; preserve the original and escalate.
distractorExplanations.c: Altering footage tampers with evidence; it must be preserved exactly as recorded.

options.a: No, without a warrant
options.b: Yes, within policy
options.c: Yes, including interrogating suspects
options.d: Only with client sign-off first

distractorExplanations.a: Guards may cooperate with lawful police requests within policy; not every request needs a warrant.
distractorExplanations.c: Helping police does not make you their interrogator; you provide facts and access within policy.
distractorExplanations.d: Policy sets when the client must be told; an emergency police request is not held for client approval.

options.a: Good customer service
options.b: Fine if they know the name
options.c: How losses happen
options.d: Required for tenants

distractorExplanations.a: Unlocking without verification is a classic social-engineering loss, not customer service.
distractorExplanations.b: Knowing a tenant's name is easy to fake; verify ID and authorization before unlocking.
distractorExplanations.d: Tenants verify identity before access; no policy requires opening suites without ID.

options.a: The client's HR to track
options.b: Optional while you are employed
options.c: Handled by your employer's renewal
options.d: Your problem on the calendar

distractorExplanations.a: The guard license is the individual's; the client's HR does not track your renewal.
distractorExplanations.b: Working with an expired card is illegal in licensing states; renewal is mandatory.
distractorExplanations.c: Employers may remind you, but the licensee is responsible for renewal and any training hours.
